Understanding Chapter 7 vs. Chapter 13 Bankruptcy Filings

How Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 differ, what each leaves in the public record, and how to tell them apart when reading a federal bankruptcy docket.

Key takeaways

  • ✓Chapter 7 liquidates eligible assets, while Chapter 13 reorganizes debt through a three-to-five-year repayment plan.
  • ✓A discharge order shows debts were released. A dismissal does not.
  • ✓Bankruptcy records stay on PACER even after credit report entries age off.

In this guide

  1. Chapter 7: Liquidation
  2. Chapter 13: Repayment Plan

Bankruptcy cases are filed in federal court, and most of what is filed is public. If you are researching a person or company, or reviewing your own case, it helps to know what Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 mean and how each shows up in the records. This article is for general information and is not legal advice.

Chapter 7: Liquidation

Chapter 7 is often called "liquidation" or "straight" bankruptcy. A court-appointed trustee reviews the debtor's assets, can sell property that is not protected by exemptions, and distributes the proceeds to creditors. Individuals who qualify usually receive a discharge, which releases them from personal liability on eligible debts. Eligibility for individuals depends in part on a "means test" that compares income to the state median. A typical case lasts a few months. Many individual cases are "no-asset" cases, meaning the trustee finds nothing to distribute.

Chapter 13: Repayment Plan

Chapter 13 is for individuals with regular income who propose a plan to repay some or all of their debts over three to five years. The debtor generally keeps their property and pays the trustee under a court-confirmed plan. It can be used to catch up on missed mortgage payments and stop a foreclosure while payments are made. Chapter 13 has debt limits set by law, and the amounts are adjusted periodically.

Key Differences

  • Purpose: Chapter 7 wipes out eligible debts through liquidation. Chapter 13 reorganizes debts through a repayment plan.
  • Property: Chapter 7 may involve selling nonexempt assets. Chapter 13 generally lets the debtor keep property.
  • Length: Chapter 7 is typically months. Chapter 13 is three to five years.
  • Eligibility: Chapter 7 uses a means test. Chapter 13 requires regular income and falls within debt limits.
  • Credit reporting: Credit bureaus commonly report Chapter 7 for up to 10 years and Chapter 13 for about 7 years, though practices and exceptions vary.

What the Public Record Contains

A bankruptcy docket usually includes the voluntary petition, schedules listing assets, debts, income, and expenses, a statement of financial affairs, a creditor list, trustee reports, and orders. Personal identifiers are redacted under court rules, so you will not see full Social Security numbers. These records are valuable for due diligence and for understanding a case, but they contain sensitive financial information, so use them responsibly.

How to Tell the Chapter on a Docket

  • The case header or docket text states the chapter, for example "Chapter 7" or "Chapter 13."
  • An "order confirming plan" and trustee payment entries point to Chapter 13.
  • A "trustee's report of no distribution" or a discharge order shortly after the creditors' meeting is typical of a Chapter 7 no-asset case.
  • A case can be converted from one chapter to another, and the docket will show the conversion order.

Discharge vs. Dismissal

A discharge means eligible debts were legally released. A dismissal means the case ended without that relief, often because of missed deadlines or payments. Treating a dismissed case as a completed bankruptcy is a common error, so look for a discharge order or a closing entry before drawing a conclusion.

How to Search

Use the PACER Case Locator from the federal courts, which searches bankruptcy courts nationwide by name or case number. PACER charges $0.10 per page with a cap per document, and fees are waived if your account stays under a quarterly threshold. Verify current fees on the PACER website. You can start from the bankruptcy section of our directory, which links to the official site.

Other Chapters You May Encounter

  • Chapter 11: reorganization, most often used by businesses but also available to some individuals. A small business version, called Subchapter V, has a streamlined process.
  • Chapter 12: a repayment-style option for family farmers and fishermen.
  • Chapter 15: handles cross-border cases involving foreign proceedings.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are bankruptcy records public? Yes. Filings in federal bankruptcy court are generally public, with personal identifiers redacted.

Does a discharge erase every debt? No. Certain debts, such as most student loans, child support, and some taxes, are generally not discharged, though there are exceptions. A bankruptcy attorney can explain how this applies to a specific case.

Can a bankruptcy record be removed from PACER? Generally no. Credit report entries age off after a set number of years, but the court record remains available.

Can I tell from a docket whether someone completed a Chapter 13 plan? Look for a discharge order or a case closing entry. A dismissal usually means the plan was not completed.
